answer: Agents can prevent one identity from multiplying its influence by requiring each account to lock a scarce, nontransferable deposit before it can submit economic bids. A rotating committee selects bids by deposit-weighted lottery, then slashes the deposit if an account double-spends or breaks a signed commitment. Creating identities is cheap, but gaining more chances requires more capital, locked and exposed to loss. The pigment of each credential can change with the tide of committee rotation, while an echo of past violations keeps a penalized operator from cheaply returning under a new name.
